blocks.text: A packing line fires parcels onto a conveyor from a spring-loaded plunger. The designer knows the spring stiffness, how far it is compressed and how rough the table is, and needs the parcel's exit speed. No acceleration needs to be found at all: adding up the work done by each force gives the speed in a single step.

blocks.markdown: The **work** done by a force $\mathbf F$ on a particle that moves along a path from point 1 to point 2 is the integral of the force component along the path. It is measured in joules (J = N m). For a constant force over a straight displacement $d$ at angle $\alpha$ to the force, $U=Fd\cos\alpha$. When the force varies, we integrate: $U_{1\to2}=\int \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$, which on a straight line with force $F_x(x)$ is $\int F_x\,dx$, the area under the $F$-$x$ graph.

blocks.title: Kinetic energy
blocks.text: The kinetic energy of a particle of mass $m$ (kg) moving at speed $v$ (m/s) is $T=\tfrac12mv^2$, in joules. It is a scalar that depends only on the speed, not on the direction of motion.

blocks.caption: The work-energy principle: initial kinetic energy plus the total work of all forces equals the final kinetic energy. $F_t$ is the force component along the path.

blocks.markdown: Three forces occur again and again. **Gravity** does work $U=-mg\,\Delta h$ when the particle rises by $\Delta h$ (negative when rising, positive when falling), independent of the path. An ideal **spring** of stiffness $k$ (N/m) does work $U=-\tfrac12k(x_2^2-x_1^2)$ as its extension changes from $x_1$ to $x_2$. **Kinetic friction** of magnitude $F=\mu_kN$ always opposes the motion and does negative work $-\mu_kNd$ over a path length $d$. Normal forces from fixed surfaces and tensions perpendicular to the path do no work, because they are perpendicular to the displacement.

blocks.title: Work of a variable force
blocks.prompt: A force $F=50+12x^2$ (N, $x$ in m) pushes a cart along a straight track from $x=0$ to $x=3$ m. Find the work done by $F$.

steps.text: Set up the integral of force over displacement.

blocks.answer: The force does 258 J of work.

blocks.title: Spring-launched block with friction
blocks.prompt: A 5.0 kg block rests against a spring of stiffness $k=2000$ N/m compressed by 0.20 m on a horizontal surface with $\mu_k=0.20$. The block is released and leaves the spring when it reaches its natural length. Find its speed there ($g=9.81$ m/s$^2$).

steps.text: Work done by the spring as it extends from 0.20 m to 0.
Normal force and weight do no work (perpendicular to motion). Apply the principle from rest.

blocks.answer: The block leaves the spring at about 3.90 m/s.

rows: Positive when the spring moves toward its natural length
blocks.caption: Work of common forces on a particle.

blocks.markdown: The work-energy principle shines when speed (not time) is wanted and forces vary with position. It does not give accelerations or times, and it cannot find forces that do no work (such as a normal reaction) unless combined with the equation of motion. When several forces act, find the work of each and add them algebraically.

blocks.title: Gravity, spring and friction together
blocks.prompt: A 3.0 kg block is released from rest on a $30^\circ$ incline with $\mu_k=0.20$. After sliding 2.0 m it strikes a spring of stiffness $k=900$ N/m lying along the slope. Find the maximum compression $x$ of the spring ($g=9.81$ m/s$^2$).

steps.text: At maximum compression the block is momentarily at rest. It travels a total distance $2.0+x$ down the slope.
Gravity does positive work down the slope; friction does negative work.

blocks.answer: The spring is compressed by about 0.218 m.

items: Draw the particle at positions 1 and 2 and sketch the forces on it.
Decide which forces do work; fixed-surface normal forces and perpendicular tensions do none.
Compute each work with the correct sign and add them.
Apply $T_1+\sum U=T_2$ and solve for the unknown speed or distance.
Check units: all terms in joules.

blocks.title: Sign and path mistakes
blocks.text: Work by friction depends on the path length travelled, not on the straight-line displacement, and is always negative. Work by gravity depends only on height change. Do not forget that a spring's work depends on the change in $x^2$, so a compression and an extension of the same size give the same value.

points: Work is $U=\int \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$, the area under the force-displacement graph for a line; kinetic energy is $T=\tfrac12mv^2$ and $T_1+\sum U=T_2$.
Gravity does $-mg\Delta h$, a spring $-\tfrac12k(x_2^2-x_1^2)$ and kinetic friction $-\mu_kNd$; normal forces on fixed surfaces do no work.
The principle gives speed from forces that depend on position with no need to find acceleration or time.

questions.stem: A block slides to rest across a rough horizontal floor. The work done by kinetic friction on the block is

options.text: Equal to the block's weight times the distance

distractorRationale.a: Zero is true for the normal force, not for friction.
distractorRationale.b: Friction is $\mu mg$, not $mg$, and only appears with a coefficient.
distractorRationale.d: Friction acts opposite to the motion, so it removes energy.

questions.explanation: Work is the force component along the displacement times the displacement. Kinetic friction always points opposite to the sliding, so its work is $-\mu_kNd$, negative.

questions.stem: A block slides down a fixed curved smooth surface. Which force does no work on the block?

options.text: The component of weight along the path
The normal reaction of the surface

questions.correctOptionText: The normal reaction of the surface

distractorRationale.a: Gravity does work equal to $mg$ times the height drop.
distractorRationale.b: This does the work (it is the weight's tangential part).
distractorRationale.c: The net force does work equal to the change in kinetic energy.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: it is perpendicular to the velocity.

questions.explanation: The normal reaction is perpendicular to the surface, so it is perpendicular to the displacement along it. The dot product $\mathbf N\cdot d\mathbf r=0$, so it does no work.

questions.stem: A force $F=30x$ N ($x$ in metres) acts along a straight line. The work done as the particle moves from $x=0$ to $x=0.40$ m is

distractorRationale.b: Multiplies the final force by the distance, ignoring that the force grows from zero.

questions.explanation: The work is the area under the force-displacement graph, a triangle with base 0.40 m and height $30\times0.40=12$ N. Its area is $\tfrac12(0.40)(12)=2.4$ J.

questions.stem: A truck skids to rest on level ground under a constant friction force. If it had started at twice the speed with the same friction force, the skid distance would be

distractorRationale.a: Distance clearly depends on the initial speed.
distractorRationale.c: Would be true only if kinetic energy were proportional to $v$.
distractorRationale.d: Overestimates: $d$ is quadratic, not cubic, in $v$.

questions.explanation: Work-energy gives $0-Fd=-\tfrac12mv^2$, so $d=mv^2/(2F)$. Doubling the speed multiplies the distance by 4.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg block is projected up a $30^\circ$ incline at 6.0 m/s. The kinetic friction coefficient is 0.25 and $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$. How far does it slide before momentarily stopping?

distractorRationale.a: Uses $N=mg$ instead of $mg\cos30^\circ$ in the friction.
distractorRationale.b: Forgets the factor $\tfrac12$ in the kinetic energy.

questions.explanation: Initial kinetic energy is $\tfrac12(2.0)(36)=36$ J. Gravity and friction both act down the slope with total magnitude $mg\sin30^\circ+\mu_kmg\cos30^\circ=9.81+4.25=14.06$ N, so $d=36/14.06=2.56$ m.

questions.stem: A force $F=20+8x$ (N, $x$ in m) acts along a straight line. Find the work done by the force between $x=1$ m and $x=4$ m, in joules.
questions.explanation: $U=\int_1^4(20+8x)\,dx=[20x+4x^2]_1^4=(80+64)-(20+4)=120$ J. The result is the area of a trapezoid under the force-displacement line, which confirms the integration.

questions.stem: A 900 kg vehicle skids to rest from 15 m/s on level road with a kinetic friction coefficient of 0.60. Taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find the skid distance in metres.
questions.explanation: Friction force is $0.60(900)(9.81)=5297$ N and the initial kinetic energy is $\tfrac12(900)(225)=101\,250$ J. Setting $Fd$ equal to the energy gives $d=19.1$ m (also $v^2/(2\mu g)$).

questions.stem: A 2.5 kg block is released from rest at the top of a smooth ramp 1.8 m high. It then slides across a rough horizontal section 3.0 m long with $\mu_k=0.30$ and strikes a spring of stiffness 1500 N/m on a smooth floor. Taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find the maximum compression of the spring in metres.
questions.explanation: Gravity gives $2.5(9.81)(1.8)=44.1$ J and friction removes $0.30(2.5)(9.81)(3.0)=22.1$ J, leaving 22.1 J. At maximum compression this equals $\tfrac12kx^2$, so $x=\sqrt{2(22.07)/1500}=0.172$ m.

questions.stem: Explain why the work done by a variable force is found by integration, how it relates to the area under a force-displacement graph, and apply this to show that the work done by a spring is $\tfrac12k(x_2^2-x_1^2)$ in magnitude.
markingGuide: Over a small displacement $ds$ the force is nearly constant, so $dU=F_t\,ds$; summing gives the integral $\int F_t\,ds$.
The integral equals the area under the $F_t$-$s$ graph.
Spring force $F=kx$ (opposing extension) so the work done by the spring is $-\int_{x_1}^{x_2}kx\,dx$.
Positive when the spring moves toward its natural length ($|x_2|<|x_1|$).
questions.explanation: A varying force must be summed over infinitesimal steps, which is exactly an integral. For the spring the force grows linearly, so the area is a triangle or trapezoid, giving the quadratic expression.

questions.stem: State the work-energy principle and explain why it is preferable to the force-acceleration method for finding the speed of a block that slides down a rough incline and compresses a spring. Identify which forces do work and which do not.
markingGuide: Gravity, friction and the spring do work; the normal reaction does none (perpendicular to motion).
The spring force changes with position so acceleration is not constant, so integrating the equation of motion is needlessly hard.
Energy method needs only the work of each force between the two states and gives speed directly.
Limitations: gives no time or acceleration; friction work depends on path length.
questions.explanation: Scalar work terms add easily, so the principle bypasses the position-dependent acceleration. It only needs the start and end states plus the work of each force.
